modern: When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, “Tomorrow perhaps you will die.”—But those are words of bad omen.—“No word is a word of bad omen,” said Epictetus, “which expresses any work of nature; or if it is, then it is also a word of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped”.
original: When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, “To-morrow perchance thou wilt die.”—But those are words of bad omen.—“No word is a word of bad omen,” said Epictetus, “which expresses any work of nature; or if it is so, it is also a word of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped”.

explained.summary:
Epictetus taught that when you kiss your child goodnight, you should quietly tell yourself they might die tomorrow. When someone objected that this was an ill-omened thing to say, he replied that nothing that describes a natural process is ill-omened, any more than talking about corn being harvested.

The practice sounds bleak, but it’s meant to make you cherish the people you love as they are now, without pretending you’ll have them forever.
explained.today: It’s the thought that might cross your mind while dropping a child at the school gate or hanging up after a call with an ageing parent. Held lightly, it isn’t morbid; it makes you less likely to waste the moment on irritation and more likely to say goodbye properly.
